name: 006-compiler-enforced
what_it_is: Frames a payload into a record and encodes it, with each set as a cargo crate so the dependency rule is a property of the manifests rather than of every source line.
the_structural_decision: Hand the rule to the compiler, then measure exactly how much of it the compiler took.

what_the_toolchain_enforces.undeclared_sibling_reference: impossible — `use tms_b64::…` is E0432 unless tms-b64 is in [dependencies]
what_the_toolchain_enforces.a_unit_compiling_alone: checkable by copying the crate to an empty directory and building it
what_the_toolchain_enforces.unused_import: a warning, and deniable at crate level

what_the_toolchain_does_NOT_enforce.declaring_a_sibling: entirely legal. Nothing in cargo objects to TMS/hex depending on TMS/b64.
what_the_toolchain_does_NOT_enforce.consequence: the site build still has to check the manifests — but ONE file per unit, in a fixed format, instead of every source line in a language the walk has to know.

SCL.policy.json: which encodings this deployment permits, and the payload cap
SCL.lib.rs: reads that file at run time, not include_str!

SMS.lib.rs: framing and unframing — the capability the program is

TMS.b64: standard base64 with padding, no dependencies
TMS.esc: printable passthrough with =XX escapes, no dependencies

DMS.lib.rs: what ran, what it cost, and the three ways a capability can be absent

non_goals: Being a serialisation library. Three encoders, a two-byte length and a sum-mod-256 checksum.
Arguing Rust is the right language for every project. The comparison this example exists to make is about the check, not about the language.
Claiming the compiler removes the need for the build's rule. Section 3 of the island test is there to show it does not.
